patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Elena Vargas is a 43-year-old left-handed Hispanic woman with a history of migraine with visual aura and hypothyroidism who presents to the emergency department with acute-onset word-finding difficulty and right arm weakness of approximately 50 minutes duration. She was at home grading papers when she noticed a zig-zag visual scotoma in her right visual field, which she recognized as her typical migraine aura. Approximately 20 minutes later, as the visual symptoms were fading, she noticed she was unable to retrieve common words — she reached for a pen but could not name it and instead said 'the thing you write with.' Simultaneously, she noticed her right arm felt heavy and clumsy, with difficulty gripping her pen. Unlike her usual migraine headache (which begins after the aura resolves and is severe and throbbing), the current headache is mild — rated 3/10. Her husband, who has witnessed her prior migraines, became alarmed because her previous auras have never caused arm weakness or speech changes and called 911. En route to hospital, EMS documented mild word-finding difficulty and right arm drift. The patient insisted she 'just needs to take her sumatriptan.' She explicitly denies chest pain, palpitations, diplopia, vertigo, dysphagia, facial numbness, loss of consciousness, or prior episodes of arm weakness. She has had no recent illness, fever, or trauma. She reports one prior first-trimester miscarriage at age 38 that was never investigated. Her mother was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus at age 45. A maternal aunt had a deep vein thrombosis at age 40. The patient takes sumatriptan for migraines and levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. She is a non-smoker, consumes minimal alcohol, is physically active, and has no known cardiovascular risk factors. She is not on oral contraceptives.

results.title: Updated Sapporo/Sydney Classification Criteria for Antiphospholipid Syndrome
results.authors: Miyakis S, Lockshin MD, et al.
results.key_finding: APS is defined by the co-occurrence of at least one clinical criterion (vascular thrombosis or obstetric complication) and at least one laboratory criterion (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM ≥40 GPL/MPL or above the 99th percentile, or anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I IgG/IgM above the 99th percentile) confirmed on two separate occasions at least 12 weeks apart.

results.title: Antiphospholipid Syndrome: AHA/ASA Statement on Stroke Prevention
results.authors: Levine SR, Brey RL, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients with stroke attributable to APS, long-term anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2-3) is preferred over antiplatelet therapy alone; triple-positive APS (lupus anticoagulant + anticardiolipin + anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I) confers the highest recurrence risk and mandates anticoagulation.

results.title: Antiphospholipid Antibodies and Stroke in Young Adults — Systematic Review
results.key_finding: Antiphospholipid antibodies are found in 10-20% of ischemic strokes in adults under age 50, compared to approximately 2-4% in older cohorts. Lupus anticoagulant is the strongest individual predictor of thrombotic risk. Triple-positive profiles carry the highest annual recurrence rate of thrombosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast head CT MUST exclude intracranial hemorrhage before IV thrombolysis is considered (tPA decision modeled through drug-interaction/contraindication check).

Coagulation results (particularly INR, platelet count, and PTT interpretation) must be available before thrombolytic decision; PTT prolongation from lupus anticoagulant must be distinguished from exogenous anticoagulation before tPA is cleared.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision

Recognize that a prolonged PTT in the absence of exogenous anticoagulant or hemophilia may reflect lupus anticoagulant — a pro-thrombotic antibody that does NOT confer bleeding risk and does NOT contraindicate IV tPA
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation

Order antiphospholipid panel (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, anti-B2GP1 IgG/IgM) in any young patient with cryptogenic stroke, particularly with personal history of miscarriage or family history of autoimmune disease
Confirm antiphospholipid antibody results on a second determination at 12 weeks to satisfy Sydney classification criteria for APS diagnosis
Plan long-term anticoagulation with warfarin (INR 2-3) if APS is confirmed — avoid DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban) which have shown higher rates of recurrent thrombosis in APS compared to VKA
Refer to rheumatology for APS classification, SLE screening, and long-term secondary prevention planning
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not withhold IV tPA solely on the basis of an elevated PTT when lupus anticoagulant is the suspected cause — lupus anticoagulant is a pro-thrombotic, not a hemorrhagic, state
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000 (100 x10^9/L), recent major surgery, or other AHA/ASA-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not diagnose complicated migraine or hemiplegic migraine without DWI MRI excluding acute infarction — new persistent focal deficits in a migraineur require full stroke workup
Do not initiate DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran) as long-term secondary prevention if APS is confirmed — VKA (warfarin) with INR 2-3 is recommended
Do not skip antiphospholipid workup in young cryptogenic stroke — APS is the underlying mechanism in 10-20% of ischemic strokes in adults under 50
key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; non-contrast CT first excludes hemorrhage and clears the tPA pathway

The migraine-with-aura history creates the central diagnostic trap: new focal deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia) in a migraineur must be treated as stroke until DWI MRI proves otherwise — complicated migraine cannot be diagnosed in the ED acutely

Lupus anticoagulant paradoxically prolongs the PTT in vitro by interfering with phospholipid-dependent coagulation assays — it is a pro-thrombotic antibody and does NOT cause bleeding; a prolonged PTT from this cause is not a contraindication to IV tPA

Mild thrombocytopenia (138 x10^9/L) in APS reflects platelet consumption by antiphospholipid antibodies — the platelet count is above the tPA threshold (<100 x10^9/L) and does not preclude thrombolysis

Triple-positive APS (lupus anticoagulant + both anticardiolipin fractions + both anti-B2GP1 fractions) carries the highest annual thrombosis recurrence risk and requires indefinite anticoagulation with warfarin

The prior miscarriage at age 38 was an obstetric criterion for APS that was never investigated — a classic missed diagnostic opportunity that this presentation forces clinicians to identify in retrospect
TOAST classification: ISCH-STR-RP04 is a stroke of other determined etiology (APS-related) — changes secondary prevention from antiplatelet to anticoagulation
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — prolonged cardiac monitoring is required regardless of APS diagnosis
MRA/CTA of intracranial and cervical vessels is normal — excludes large-artery atherosclerosis, dissection, and LVO, all of which must be ruled out before attributing the stroke to APS
Antiphospholipid antibody testing must be confirmed at 12 weeks to meet Sydney classification criteria — a single positive result is insufficient for definitive APS diagnosis
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle — 43-year-old left-handed Hispanic woman with migraine-with-aura history presenting with right arm weakness and anomic aphasia. Patient and bystanders initially attribute symptoms to complicated migraine. MRI DWI confirms acute left MCA cortical infarct. Paradoxically prolonged PTT and mild thrombocytopenia create compounding decision-points. Systematic workup including antiphospholipid panel reveals triple-positive APS as the underlying mechanism. Real case seeded from Cureus 2024 (PMID 38659540), a 43-year-old woman with triple-positive APS and left MCA territory ischemic stroke.
metadata.real_seed_note: Case seeded from: Cureus 2024 (PMC11042755, PMID 38659540, CC-BY 4.0). Original case: 43-year-old woman, triple-positive APS (lupus anticoagulant dRVVT 1.92/1.97, anticardiolipin IgG 90.9 GPL, IgM 23.7 MPL, anti-B2GP1 IgG 21.0, IgM 10.0 U/mL), acute left MCA cortical infarct (left superior parietal and posterior insula), treated with IV alteplase with improvement to NIHSS 0. Antiphospholipid antibody values, ECG (normal sinus rhythm), echo (normal), and lipid panel adapted directly from the published case. Demographics, HPI, migraine history, miscarriage history, family history of SLE, and red herring elements authored for NeuroBench narrative fidelity and puzzle construction.
clinical_pearls: Migraine with aura and acute ischemic stroke can be indistinguishable in the first 30 minutes — DWI MRI is the only reliable discriminator; always pursue stroke workup when deficits are motor or aphasic

Lupus anticoagulant prolongs the PTT in vitro by interfering with phospholipid-dependent assay steps but is a pro-thrombotic antibody in vivo — it is the strongest individual predictor of APS-related thrombosis

Triple-positive APS (all three antibody classes positive simultaneously) is the highest-risk APS profile and mandates indefinite anticoagulation; DOACs have demonstrated higher failure rates than warfarin in APS-related thrombosis

Obstetric APS criteria (recurrent miscarriage, fetal loss, placental insufficiency) are frequently missed prior to a thrombotic event — a history of unexplained miscarriage in a young woman with stroke should trigger APS workup

APS affects approximately 10-20% of young adults with cryptogenic ischemic stroke — it is one of the most important treatable stroke mechanisms in patients under 50 with no traditional vascular risk factors
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Triple-positive APS as hidden stroke mechanism in a migraineur; paradoxical PTT prolongation that mimics anticoagulation; mild thrombocytopenia distracting from APS; normal vascular imaging and cardiac workup; requires antiphospholipid panel to unlock diagnosis.
